name: Igbo-Ukwu culture
title: The story of the Igbo-Ukwu culture

text: More than 1,000 years ago, people lived at Igbo-Ukwu, in south-eastern Nigeria.
Its name means “Great Igbo”, and its finds are linked with the Nri-Igbo people.
src: 9th century CE: Bronzes, beads and a rich burial are placed at Igbo-Ukwu / Igbo-Ukwu, a town in Anambra State, south-eastern Nigeria
the town of Igbo-Ukwu, “Great Igbo” / the sites are associated with the Nri-Igbo

text: Their metalworkers cast bronze pots, crowns and ornaments covered in tiny, fine details.
Even small insects that landed on the surface were cast into some pieces.
src: lost-wax bronzes with fine surface detail, among them ritual vessels, pendants, crowns, breastplates / The bronzes were made by lost-wax casting
small insects that seem to have landed on the surface were cast in one piece with the vessel

text: In the Nsukka region nearby, people had already made iron for more than 2,000 years.
Most of the metal for the bronzes came from old mines about 100 kilometres away.
src: c. 2000 BCE: Iron is smelted at Lejja in the Nsukka region, about 100 kilometres east of Igbo-Ukwu
analysis showed that most of the metal came from mines about 100 kilometres away

text: Archaeologists found about 165,000 beads of glass, carnelian and other stone.
Some glass beads came through trade from as far as Egypt, Iran and Mesopotamia.
src: about 165,000 glass, carnelian and stone beads
Glass beads from as far as Mesopotamia, Iran and Egypt show that Igbo-Ukwu was tied into long-distance trade

text: Isaiah Anozie found the first bronzes at his home and used some pots to water his goats.
Experts first doubted they were made there, but tests proved them local, and some are now in the British Museum.
src: Isaiah Anozie, who found the first bronzes while digging in his compound in 1938 / used some of the vessels to water his goats
experts first doubted they were local / Isotope analysis and radiocarbon dating proved them local and far older / Five objects from Isaiah Anozie’s first finds are in the British Museum
